Federal Auditor Finds Ottawa Quietly Dropped Thermal Coal Export Ban Without Public Notice

31 Oct 2026, 07:31 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Climate Desk · Source: www.cbc.ca

3 min read

Key takeawaysA newly tabled federal audit reveals that Environment and Climate Change Canada quietly abandoned its initiative to end thermal coal exports, doing so without any public announcement or formal ministerial record of direction.

Image: www.cbc.ca · Photo source · Cropped to 16:9; original source image

In this article
  1. Timeline of Policy Shift and Industry Lobbying
  2. International Commitments and U.S. Transit
  3. Practical Implications and Reader Verification

A newly tabled federal audit reveals that Environment and Climate Change Canada quietly abandoned its initiative to end thermal coal exports, doing so without any public announcement or formal ministerial record of direction.

According to the report from the Office of the Auditor General, tabled on Thursday, the federal department spent three years attempting to establish an enforcement mechanism for the export ban, which was originally committed to in 2021 as part of broader environmental goals. Burning thermal coal remains one of the most carbon-intensive forms of electricity generation globally.

Timeline of Policy Shift and Industry Lobbying

The audit highlights that work on the export ban steadily diminished following heavy lobbying from the coal industry. Although regulatory enforcement efforts began in late 2021—with officials examining potential pathways under toxic substance regulations akin to single-use plastics frameworks—those efforts shifted toward voluntary measures by February 2024.

By November 2024, all internal work on the ban ceased entirely. Auditors noted that the department produced no official documentation or written direction ordering the termination of the project at that time. The decision was formalized later in August 2025 under government-wide cost-saving measures, yet the public was never informed. Compounding the issue, the audit revealed that Environment and Climate Change Canada failed to notify Global Affairs Canada of the cancellation, despite Global Affairs having provided trade risk assessments linked to the proposed ban.

International Commitments and U.S. Transit

The policy reversal stands in contrast to Canada's position as co-chair of an international alliance dedicated to transitioning away from coal. While domestic export restriction efforts stalled, the federal government continued major international funding commitments. These include $15 billion pledged to the Women-Led Coal Transition Mechanism and a $1 billion low-interest loan allocation to the Climate Investment Funds' Accelerating Coal Transition program.

Furthermore, the audit reported that thermal coal exports from Canadian ports actually increased in 2025 compared to 2021 levels. Approximately 61 per cent of the thermal coal shipped from Canadian ports in 2025 originated in the United States—primarily from Washington, Oregon, and California—transported north by rail to British Columbia shipping terminals due to domestic U.S. regulatory hurdles for Pacific coast export infrastructure.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

For industry stakeholders, provincial governments, labor organizations, and shipping authorities, the lack of transparency complicates long-term planning for a just transition.

Confirmed Details:

  • Environment and Climate Change Canada stopped all internal work on a thermal coal export ban in November 2024.
  • No public announcement of the cancellation was made, and the decision was formally tied to cost-saving measures in August 2025.
  • Approximately 61 per cent of thermal coal passing through Canadian ports in 2025 came from the United States.

Uncertain Details:

  • The exact nature of the non-voluntary or voluntary measures considered before work stopped entirely remains unspecified in public records.
  • The full long-term impact on international trade partnerships and domestic labor forces without a structured transition plan has not been formally assessed by the department.

Readers can verify these findings by reviewing the complete audit documentation directly through the Office of the Auditor General of Canada.
